en: Sutta Nipāta 4.16 Sāriputtasutta “Never before have I seen [one such as this].”
(Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Nor have I heard it from anyone else:
such is the Teacher who speaks so beautifully."
The one from the Tuṣita heaven has come to the assembly;
he appears to the world with its devas like one who possesses sight.
Having dispelled all darkness,
he alone attained delight.
To that Buddha, unattached and such-like—
I have come to this assembly;
for many who are bound here,
there is a purpose for my coming with this question.
For a bhikkhu who feels revulsion [for worldly things],
who frequents empty dwellings—
the foot of a tree or a charnel ground—
Or in caves among the mountains—
among these various high and low couches,
how many terrors are there?
The monk who would not be shaken by noise while in his lodging—
how many perils are there in the world?
For the monk who overcomes [the defilements] while dwelling in a remote lodging, there is no direction he goes that is not already traversed.
What would be his modes of address?
What would be his spheres of activity here?
What would be his vows and observances?
For a bhikkhu who is resolute,
having undertaken what training,
being unified, wise, and mindful?
“Just as a smith blows away the dross from silver,
so should one blow away the impurities from oneself.
For one who is practicing self-repulsion, this is what constitutes well-being.
(Sāriputta, said the Blessed One:
"If one who desires full enlightenment practices according to the Dhamma, resorting to a seat and a bed that are empty;"
I shall explain that to you according to my understanding:
a wise bhikkhu, mindful and living within the bounds of restraint, should not fear the five fears.
One should not be terrified of gadflies and mosquitoes, of reptiles,
of the touch of humans, of quadrupeds,
nor even of those who follow other doctrines.
Even having seen those many terrors,
one who seeks what is wholesome should further encounter other perils.
Touched by the touch of illness and by hunger,
he should endure cold and heat;
though touched by these in many ways, he remains homeless.
One should exert firm energy and strive.
One should neither commit theft nor speak falsehoods.
One should touch all beings, both moving and stationary, with loving-kindness.
When one recognizes that the mind has become defiled,
one should dispel it as being on the side of darkness.
One should not fall under the power of anger and arrogance.
One should stand having dug up even their very roots;
whether it be pleasant or unpleasant,
you will surely experience the consequences.
Placing wisdom foremost and possessing noble joy,
one should suppress those dangers;
one should overcome aversion while lying down in a secluded place.
One should overcome the four states that lead to lamentation:
"What shall I eat? Where shall I eat? Alas, it is difficult to lie down! Where shall I lie down today?"
These thoughts are fit for lamentation;
the trainee, wandering without a home, should dispel them.
Having obtained food and clothing at the proper time, [he should remain mindful].
He should know the proper measure here for the sake of contentment;
guarded among those [people] and restrained in his conduct in the village,
even when provoked, he should not utter harsh speech.
With downcast eyes and not fidgeting with his feet,
devoted to meditation, wide awake,
and having established himself in equanimity with a concentrated mind.
One should cut off the underlying tendency toward doubt and remorse.
When reproached with words, the mindful one should rejoice;
he should break down the barrenness of heart toward his fellow celibates.
One should utter wholesome speech, not excessively;
one should not intend to engage in idle talk about people.
Furthermore, there are five stains in the world:
Those who, being mindful, train in discipline—
let them subdue passion for forms, sounds, and likewise tastes, smells, and touches.
Having removed desire for these phenomena,
the mindful bhikkhu, with a well-liberated mind,
should at the proper time thoroughly investigate the Dhamma correctly.
"Becoming one-pointed, he shall dispel the darkness.
Thus ends the sixteenth discourse, the Sāriputta Sutta.
This is the fourth chapter, the Aṭṭhaka Vagga.
Its summary verse:
Desire, the cave, and the corrupt,
the pure, and supreme old age.
Metteyya and Pasūra,
Māgaṇḍiya and Purābheda;
Kalaha and the two Byūhas.
Furthermore, the Tuvaṭṭaka;
the Attadaṇḍa-sutta, the foremost;
and sixteen [verses] asked by the Elder.
Thus, these suttas are all those of the Aṭṭhakavagga.
